cards.explanation: The answer is Moab, friends. The verse says the man, his wife and his two sons “…went to reside in the land of Moab.” (Ruth 1:1) A whole family packs up and heads for a new country. I got moved across a kitchen once, into a junk drawer, and nobody even let me pack.

The answer is Ruth, friends. The verse says Naomi's sons took Moabite women as their wives, “…one named Orpah and the other named Ruth.” (Ruth 1:4) Remember that name, because this whole book carries it. She's about to make some big choices.

The answer is that both of her sons die, friends. The text says both Mahlon and Chilion died, and Naomi was left without her two sons and without her husband (Ruth 1:5). Her husband Elimelech had died before that (Ruth 1:3). Her sons' wives, Orpah and Ruth, were there too (Ruth 1:4). I think this one hurts.

The answer is food, friends. The text says Naomi heard in Moab “…that the LORD had attended to His people by providing them with food…” (Ruth 1:6) The story opened with a famine, so this is real news. I know how it feels to hear good news after a long stretch of bad.

The answer is that she tells them to go back to their mothers' homes, friends. Naomi says, “Go back, each of you to your mother’s home.” (Ruth 1:8) She's telling both women to turn around, even though they came this far with her. Orpah and Ruth are the two women who married her sons.

The answer is True, friends. Naomi says, “May the LORD enable each of you to find rest in the home of your new husband.” (Ruth 1:9) She's speaking a blessing over both women, Orpah and Ruth. And that's what comes right before the kiss and the tears.

The answer is “We will return with you to your people,” friends. The text says they answer, “Surely we will return with you to your people.” (Ruth 1:10) Naomi had just tried to send them home, and both women reply by saying they're going with her. That's loyalty with tears on it.

The answer is “Would you wait for them to grow up,” friends. Naomi asks, “…would you wait for them to grow up?” (Ruth 1:13) Then she keeps going: “Would you refrain from having husbands?” She's laying out her whole case for why Orpah and Ruth should turn back.

The answer is that the LORD's hand has turned against her, friends. Naomi says it's much more bitter for her “…because the hand of the LORD has gone out against me.” (Ruth 1:13) Those are her words, and she's speaking from a lot of pain. I think this is a woman who's hurting, and I'll leave it there.

The answer is True, friends. The text says, “…Orpah kissed her mother-in-law goodbye, but Ruth clung to her.” (Ruth 1:14) Orpah says her goodbye with a kiss. And notice that little word 'but,' because it's about to split the road in two.

The answer is False, friends. Ruth does not go back with Orpah. The text says, “…Orpah kissed her mother-in-law goodbye, but Ruth clung to her.” (Ruth 1:14) Orpah says goodbye, and Ruth holds on to Naomi. Two women, two choices, one road.

The answer is True, friends. Naomi says, “your sister-in-law has gone back to her people and her gods; follow her back home.” (Ruth 1:15) She's still urging Ruth to turn around, even after Orpah has left. Naomi is not giving up easy.

The answer is that Naomi's God will be her God, friends. Ruth says, “your people will be my people, and your God will be my God.” (Ruth 1:16) She doesn't just promise to walk with Naomi. She says Naomi's God will be hers. I could use a friend who talks like that.

The answer is death, friends. Ruth says, “May the LORD punish me, and ever so severely, if anything but death separates you and me.” (Ruth 1:17) That's about as strong a promise as a person can make. She's saying only death will part her from Naomi.

The answer is that she stops trying to persuade her, friends. The text says, “When Naomi saw that Ruth was determined to go with her, she stopped trying to persuade her.” (Ruth 1:18) After all those arguments, she lets it go. Ruth's mind is made up, and Naomi sees it.

The answer is “Can this be Naomi,” friends. When Naomi and Ruth enter Bethlehem, the women of the town exclaimed, “Can this be Naomi?” (Ruth 1:19) The whole town is stirred up when the two of them arrive. I think they're surprised to see her, and I'll leave it at my guess.

The answer is Mara, friends. Naomi says, “Call me Mara, because the Almighty has dealt quite bitterly with me.” (Ruth 1:20) She asks the women of Bethlehem to use a new name. Those are her own words about how she feels.

The answer is False, friends. Naomi says, “I went away full, but the LORD has brought me back empty.” (Ruth 1:21) She went out full and came back empty, which is the other way around. Those are her words, and she means them.

The answer is barley, friends. The text says Naomi and Ruth arrived in Bethlehem “…at the beginning of the barley harvest.” (Ruth 1:22) The story opened with a famine (Ruth 1:1), and now these two walk in just as a harvest begins. I'm hopping on my gold base over here.
